site_faq_a_what_is_tka: Notation for flow arts: a way to write prop movement down instead of relying on video alone. Each step becomes one pictograph showing hand positions on a grid, the motion each hand makes, and the prop's orientation. String them together and you have choreography you can read, edit, and hand to another spinner.
site_faq_q_memorize: Do I have to memorize letters and symbols first?
site_faq_a_memorize: No. Pictographs read visually: the grid shows where your hands can be, the arrows show where they go. The letters are names for patterns, useful once you want to compare and remix sequences. Nothing needs to be memorized before you can follow along.
site_faq_q_video: I learn moves from videos. Why would I need notation?
site_faq_a_video: Video shows one performance from one angle. Notation shows the structure underneath it. Once a sequence is written down you can change one step and see exactly what follows, trade it with someone who has never seen the original, or come back in a year and read it cold. A recording and sheet music do different jobs. Musicians keep both.
site_faq_q_first_prop: I've never spun a prop. Where do I start?
site_faq_a_first_prop: Double staves. TKA was designed around them: each staff has two ends, one is your thumb reference and one is your pinky reference, and with proper technique those references never change. That is what makes prop orientation readable while you learn. Grab a pair of staves and start with the Level 1 guide.
site_faq_q_props: Does it work with my prop?
site_faq_a_props: Double staves are the canonical prop. TKA also applies to dual-wielded static props such as fans, clubs, and buugeng. Momentum-based props, tosses, contact rolling, and grip changes are not covered as equals. Composer includes additional prop visuals, but a visual option does not mean every movement applies to that prop.
site_faq_note_poi: Poi can follow the notation with steady rotation, and the poi notation page shows where momentum draws the line.
site_faq_q_software: Is there software for flow arts choreography?
site_faq_a_software: Yes. Flow Arts Composer is free flow arts software that runs in your browser. Build sequences step by step, generate them from parameters, animate the result, save it, and share it. Each sequence keeps its Kinetic Alphabet notation, so the structure remains visible beside the animation.
site_faq_a_free: Yes. Flow Arts Composer is currently free to use. Premium is not live. You can build sequences, animate them, save your work, and browse the community library without paying.
site_faq_q_share: Can I share what I make?
site_faq_a_share: Yes. Export a sequence as a PNG or video. On supported phones, the system share sheet can send the file to another app. You can also share a sequence link, and eligible saved sequences can be published to the community gallery.

create_tour_help_generation_mode_full_de: Determines whether your sequence loops back to its starting placement or ends freely.
create_tour_help_generation_mode_tip: LOOP sequences are great for practice because you can repeat them seamlessly.

create_tour_help_grid_mode_bullet_2: Box: Hands on intercardinal points (NE, SE, SW, NW)

create_tour_help_length_bullet_2: LOOP mode: 4-64 steps (must be even for symmetry)
create_tour_help_length_full_desc: Sets how many steps (individual moves) your generated sequence will have. Each step is one pictograph showing a single movement.
create_tour_help_length_tip: Shorter sequences are easier to learn and memorize.
create_tour_help_level_full_desc: Controls how many additional turns your props can do during each step.
create_tour_help_level_tip: Start at Level 1 to learn the base motions, then progress to Level 3 for the full vocabulary.
create_tour_help_loop_type_bullet_1: Rotated: Placements rotate around the grid center
create_tour_help_loop_type_bullet_2: Mirrored: Second half mirrors the first (left↔right)
create_tour_help_loop_type_bullet_3: Swapped: Hands switch roles in the return (blue↔red)
create_tour_help_loop_type_bullet_5: Combinations: Mix multiple types for complex patterns

create_tour_help_loop_type_tip: Try different LOOP types with the same settings to see how they change the feel.
create_tour_help_period_bullet_1: Halved: Sequence splits into 2 parts - simpler, more obvious loop point
create_tour_help_period_bullet_2: Quartered: Sequence splits into 4 parts - more complex, subtler transitions

create_tour_help_period_tip: Halved is easier to follow. Quartered creates more intricate patterns.
create_tour_help_prop_continuity_bullet_: Continuous: Props keep spinning the same direction - smooth, flowing movements

create_tour_help_prop_continuity_full_de: Controls whether props maintain their spinning direction or can reverse mid-sequence.
create_tour_help_prop_continuity_tip: Continuous is easier to execute. Reversals add visual interest but require more control.

create_tour_help_start_end_bullet_2: End Placement: (Freeform only) Force the sequence to end at a specific placement

create_tour_help_turn_intensity_full_des: Limits the maximum number of additional turns per step. Lower intensity means gentler, simpler movements.

guide_welcome_what: You've come across The Kinetic Alphabet, a notation system designed to help you craft and communicate your own unique choreography. This grid-based language is designed for music, using pictographs and letters that combine like puzzle pieces for each step. This system has propelled my sequence creation to new heights, and I hope it will do the same for you!

guide_l2_double_turns_intro: Level 2 chapter on 2-turns: 360° prop rotations on shifts, dashes, and static motions, plus the codex reference pages for double-turning letters.
guide_l2_topic_double_turn_dashes_descri: Now let's add a double turn to a dash. It's relatively complex, so we'll break it down into four parts.
guide_l2_topic_double_turn_shifts_descri: 2 turns add a 360 degree rotation to a motion.
guide_l2_topic_double_turn_static_descri: A static motion with 2 turns is simply a 360° turn in place. It's necessary to use negative space or a turn to achieve this.
guide_l2_topic_glyphs_pads_description: A glyph is a letter combined with other characters, such as numbers or symbols.
guide_l2_topic_one_one_turns_description: For a turn on both props, add a "1" in both the high and the low slot. This can also be written as 1|1.
guide_l2_topic_opening_closing_descripti: Because of Gamma's asymmetry, Λ (Lam) presents an extra variation when adding a turn.
guide_l2_topic_s_and_t_description: S and T are a different type of hybrid. Even though their motions are a matching shift type (pro|pro, anti|anti), each has one hand leading and the other following.
guide_l2_topic_turn_shifts_description: A turn is a 180° rotation that occurs during a motion. Let's add a single turn to a shift.
guide_l2_topic_turns_dashes_static_descr: You can also add a turn to a dash. During the prop rotation, move the hand directly in a straight line.
guide_l2_topic_types_1_6_turns_descripti: When motion types are exactly the same, put left in the high slot and right in the low slot.

guide_paths_awkward: When the drawing works but the motion doesn’t
guide_paths_awkward_advice: Watch those joins in the animation, including the return to the first step. Compare Arc with Concave, then try a per-hand exception in Composer. Keep the path that suits the movement you want to perform.
guide_paths_awkward_body: A mandala shows the whole trace at once. It can hide a sharp change where two steps meet.
guide_paths_compare: Pick a matrix cell, then compare Arc with Hybrid. When one hand is pro and the other anti, they follow different kinds of paths. Switch the trace between Hands and Prop tips to see what the prop’s rotation adds.

guide_paths_exceptions: Dashes stay straight. Static hands stay at their grid point, even when the prop rotates. Float uses the underlying fixed path when Hybrid is on.
guide_paths_hybrid_definition: Pro motions use Arc. Anti motions use Concave.
guide_paths_linear_definition: The hand takes a straight line between the endpoints.
guide_paths_lines: Path lines are the drawn guides. You can hide them while keeping the same movement.

guide_paths_third_order_body: The hand’s path can be a motion of its own. In Third Order, a moving grid carries another sequence. The outer motion moves the grid; the inner sequence moves within it.
guide_paths_third_order_concave: The current Concave option bends an arc inward. It is not an exact four-petal antispin construction. Use the flower carrier in Third Order when you want to work with the constructed path and its spin ratio.
guide_paths_third_order_explore: Explore extension and antispin by starting with circular travel, then trying a flower as the carrier path. A flower can be built from two rotations before the prop adds its own rotation.

guide_paths_try_four_body: Switch the path while the sequence plays. Hybrid uses Arc for pro motions and Concave for anti motions. Any motion can take any path; Hybrid only sets the default.
guide_paths_what_changes_body: A path sets how a hand travels between its positions. The sequence keeps its letters and turns.
guide_prospin_anti_definition: The prop rotates in the opposite direction of the handpath.
guide_prospin_intro: Prospin and Inspin name the same motion: the prop rotates the same direction as the handpath. Most poi spinners say Inspin. The Kinetic Alphabet says Prospin.

guide_prospin_why_orientation: In and out already name orientations here, like thumb in and thumb out, so Inspin reads like one of them. Pro isn't an orientation. Prospin only says which way the prop spins.
guide_prospin_why_pair: Pro and anti are opposites, with and against, so the pair sorts every shift the way the motion does: with the handpath or against it.

guide_ratios_intro: A spin ratio counts one pattern twice: how many circles the hand travels, and how many rotations the prop makes over the same span. It is written hands first, so 1:3 is one hand circle to three prop rotations. The Kinetic Alphabet counts the same motion as turns, where one turn is 180 degrees of prop rotation on top of the base rotation the motion already carries.
guide_ratios_ladder_intro: Every turn value the Kinetic Alphabet carries, set out by the level that first allows it. Each card gives the ratio, the turns it names, and the two flowers one hand draws at that ratio, following one end of the prop. A level keeps everything the levels before it allow and adds the cards under it.
guide_ratios_ladder_orientation: Through Level 3 each ratio shows four flowers: prospin and antispin, each from a start with the prop pointing in and a start pointing out. At Level 1 those are four different base motions. From Level 2 on, the second start draws the first flower turned half a petal, so each flower is named by how it sits: a petal pointing up or down, petals stacked vertical or lying horizontal, four petals in diamond or box. At Level 4's quarter turns both starts draw the very same flower, so those cards show one, and every one of them puts a petal straight down, prospin and antispin alike.

guide_ratios_twelve_example: The 1:1 prospin pair shows what the start does most plainly. Starting in holds the tracked end of the prop in one place, so it draws a point. Starting out carries that end around the whole hand circle. On a staff the two starts are the two ends of one prop, so the twelve fold into six.
guide_ratios_twelve_intro: Nichols took four even petaled driving styles from each family, which gives twelve shapes for one hand. Three ratios, two spin directions, and two starting orientations reach the same twelve: prospin or antispin, started in or started out. A start pointing in puts the prop toward the center of the hand path, a start pointing out puts it away, and that choice moves where the figure sits.
guide_ratios_whole_turn_note: Each whole turn adds two petals to both flowers, and a half turn adds one, so Level 3 fills the gaps between these counts.

guide_l2_glyphs_intro: A glyph is a letter combined with other characters, such as numbers or symbols.
guide_l2_glyphs_slots: To the right of each letter, there are two slots: high and low. These slots contain numbers that indicate turns.
guide_l2_glyphs_update: TKA software now handles the placement of these numbers, so it's less important that you learn this. Don't sweat it. Focus on the motions.
guide_l2_glyphs_hybrid: In a hybrid, motion types are different and must be disambiguated. These rules indicate where to place numbers:
guide_l2_glyphs_order_before: The motion that is higher on the list is indicated by the high slot. Remember the order with the acronym
guide_l2_glyphs_st: The letters S and T have another factor, leading/following. In their case, leading is high and following is low.
guide_l2_glyphs_five_hybrids: There are five hybrids, each shown below in their corresponding high/low slots:
guide_l2_glyphs_remaining: The remaining letters have combinations of the same motion type. For these, put left in the high slot and right in the low slot.
guide_l2_type6_intro: Finally, Type 6 letters have both hands remaining static. Both types are the same (static|static), so the number goes in the high slot by default.
guide_l2_type6_letters: This includes α, β, and Γ.
guide_l2_type6_arrow: Note that the arrow can follow the path of either the thumb end or pinky end. The optimal placement depends on context.
guide_l2_type6_next: These static single-turns are relatively simple. Next we'll look at dual-turns, in which both props are receiving a turn.
guide_l2_type5_intro: In Type 5 motions, both hands are dashing, so there are no hybrids. Since they're the same type (dash|dash), the left goes in the high slot, and the right goes in the low slot.
guide_l2_type5_letters: This includes Φ-, Ψ-, and Λ-.
guide_l2_type5_slots: Remember, the high/low slots do not refer to left/right. Instead, their purpose is to differentiate two motion types. In Type 5, those motion types are the same (dash|dash).
guide_l2_type5_practice: As always, pause at the halfway point to drill it into your muscle memory. This will ensure proper timing.
guide_l2_type4_intro: Type 4 hybrids combine a dash with a static motion. There is no shift involved. According to PADS, a dash is higher than a static motion.
guide_l2_type4_slots: For Type 4, high = dash and low = static. This includes Φ, Ψ, and Λ.
guide_l2_type4_code: When typing the words for sequences containing greek symbols, it's easier to just type the word or its first three letters. E.g. "phi(0,1)". The corresponding symbol can easily be swapped in with a simple script. The short versions of the seven greek letters are "sig, del, the, om, phi, psi, lam"
guide_l2_codex_pages_intro: Reference grids showing all letters at each turn combination.
guide_l2_type3_intro: Type 3 hybrids combine a shift with a dash. When we consult PADS, we find that a shift is higher than a dash, therefore:
guide_l2_type3_slots: For Type 3, high = shift and low = dash. This includes W-, X-, Y-, Z-, Σ-, Δ-, Θ-, and Ω-.
guide_l2_type3_halfway: Take note of this strange position at the halfway point. There is a hand-to-end relationship between the left hand and the right staff's pinky end. It is important to pass through this position for the timing to be accurate.
guide_l2_type3_dash_turn: Now let's add 1 turn to the dash, leaving the shifting hand unmodified. This creates a rotational relationship, so we'll need to use Same-dots and Opp-dots.
guide_l2_type3_center: The halfway position holds the key for executing cross-shifts with accurate timing. Though unfamiliar now, these centric positions will be thoroughly deconstructed later on.
guide_l2_type3_code: When writing code, put the dash after the letter and before the parentheses. E.g. Z-(s,0,1)
guide_l2_type2_intro: Type 2 hybrids combine a shift and a static motion. These two motion types are different, so we use the high/low slots to differentiate them. To determine where they go, remember PADS. Because a shift (pro/anti) is higher than a static motion, we can confidently state that:
guide_l2_type2_slots: For Type 2, high = shift and low = static. This includes W, X, Y, Z, Σ, Δ, Θ, and Ω.
guide_l2_type2_relationship: Type 2 motions become more complex when we add turns to the static hand. Since this causes both props to rotate, it creates either a Same or Opposite relationship. To indicate this, add a dot above or below the letter. A same-dot goes above and an opp-dot goes below.
guide_l2_type2_code: You can also use (s) or (o) as parameters to indicate "same" or "opp". E.g. "W(s,0,1)"
guide_l2_type1_same: When motion types are exactly the same, put left in the high slot and right in the low slot. Here is a breakdown of A¹ (pro|pro) and B¹ (anti|anti).
guide_l2_type1_hybrids: When motion types are different, high/low indicates how to label them. With hybrids, we can add a turn to either the pro or anti motion.
guide_l2_type1_slots: For pro/anti hybrids, high = prospin and low = antispin. This includes C, F, I, L, O, R, U, and V.
guide_l2_type1_code: For code or file-naming, indicate turns with parentheses like so: C¹ = C(1,0) and C₁ = C(0,1)
guide_l2_st_intro: S and T are a different type of hybrid. Even though their motions are a matching shift type (pro|pro, anti|anti), each has one hand leading and the other following. Though this doesn't affect their base forms, it produces additional variations when modifying their motions. S and T are the only letters that have a leader and follower while both hands share the same motion type.
guide_l2_st_slots: Fortunately, we have a tool to disambiguate hybrids: the high/low slots. For S and T, high = leading and low = following.
guide_l2_st_s_high_caption: S-High-One - both hands prospin; the leading hand carries the turn, the following hand only travels
guide_l2_st_s_low_caption: S-Low-One - both hands prospin; the following hand carries the turn, the leading hand only travels
guide_l2_st_t_high_caption: T-High-One - both hands antispin; the leading hand carries the turn, the following hand only travels
guide_l2_st_t_low_caption: T-Low-One - both hands antispin; the following hand carries the turn, the leading hand only travels
guide_l2_st_uv_exception: Note that these leading/following rules do NOT apply to U and V. Even though U and V have a leader/follower, their slots refer to pro/anti.
guide_l2_open_close_intro: Because of Gamma's asymmetry, Λ (Lam) presents an extra variation when adding a turn. We can't use rotational relationship to tell them apart, because there isn't one to describe. Instead, we can disambiguate them with opening and closing. This refers to the appearance of the 90° angle if we continue the rotation into a pro-shift.
guide_l2_open_close_high_open_caption: Opening - the dashing hand carries the turn; its spin resolves toward alpha, hands finishing apart
guide_l2_open_close_high_close_caption: Closing - the dashing hand carries the turn; its spin resolves toward beta, hands finishing together
guide_l2_open_close_static_turn: Now let's add 1 turn to the static hand, leaving the dash in its base form. Since the dashing prop is not rotating, there is no rotational relationship to describe. However the rotating static prop can still be identified as opening or closing.
guide_l2_open_close_low_open_caption: Opening - the static hand carries the turn this time; its spin resolves toward alpha, hands finishing apart
guide_l2_open_close_low_close_caption: Closing - the static hand carries the turn this time; its spin resolves toward beta, hands finishing together
guide_l2_open_close_speech: It's not necessary to speak all of the glyph modifications when talking about a letter. It would be cumbersome if you were required to say "Lam-Low-One-Closing". In the context of a word or sequence, you can just refer to the base letter "Lam" instead.
guide_l2_open_close_code: To shorten this for code, include "op" or "cl" as a final parameter. E.g. "(0,1,op)" or "(0,1,cl)"
guide_l2_one_one_intro: For a turn on both props, add a "1" in both the high and the low slot. This can also be written as 1|1. Here are some cherry-picked examples of 1|1 in each Type. Since you know all the mechanisms involved, explanation is kept to a minimum.
guide_l2_one_one_practice: Pause at the halfway point of each motion while learning. This will ensure accurate timing.
guide_l2_one_one_d_caption: D-One-One - both hands prospin together, watch them turn in sync, ending with thumbs out
guide_l2_one_one_i_caption: I-One-One - one hand prospins while the other antispins at the same time, ending with mixed thumb references
guide_l2_one_one_n_caption: N-One-One - both hands antispin together, watch them turn in sync, ending with thumbs in
guide_l2_one_one_v_caption: V-One-One - one hand antispins while the other prospins at the same time, ending with mixed thumb references
guide_l2_dashes_intro: Add a turn to a dash. Move the hand straight as the prop turns and pause halfway to check the center position.
guide_l2_dashes_caption: The staff travels straight from south to north and changes thumb orientation.
guide_l2_dashes_thumb_switches: A base dash has one thumb switch (in → out). With one turn it has two (in → in).
guide_l2_dashes_extension: This repeated motion is called a linear extension. Focus on the antispin half to keep the hand path straight.
guide_l2_static_intro: Finally, look at a static turn starting with the thumb in.
guide_l2_static_caption: The staff stays at east while its thumb reference changes from in to out.
guide_l2_static_any_point: Do this at any hand point, from either thumb orientation and in either rotation direction.
guide_l2_static_arrow_intro: Compare the arrows for static turns and prospin turns:
guide_l2_static_arrow: The prop stays at its starting position. The arrow forms a semicircle around it.
guide_l2_shift_arrow: The prop ends at an adjacent position. The arrow forms a semicircle around the empty start position.
guide_l2_shifts_intro: A turn is a 180° rotation during a motion. Add one turn to a shift.
guide_l2_shifts_pro_intro: First add one turn to a prospin. Pause at the diagonal halfway position. The arrow follows the pinky end first, then the thumb end, forming a semicircle from the outer start point.
guide_l2_shifts_pro_caption: Prospin: the staff turns with its arc as it shifts from east to south.
guide_l2_shifts_thumb_rule: Each turn adds a thumb switch.
guide_l2_shifts_pro_thumb: An isolation has no thumb switch. A prospin with one turn has one (in → out).
guide_l2_shifts_anti_intro: Now add one turn to an antispin. Pause again at the diagonal halfway position.
guide_l2_shifts_anti_caption: Antispin: the staff turns against its arc as it shifts from east to south.
guide_l2_shifts_anti_thumb: A base antispin has one thumb switch (in → out). With one turn it has two (in → out → in).
guide_l2_double_static_intro: A static motion with two turns rotates 360° in place. Use negative space or a turn to make room.
guide_l2_double_static_caption: At east, the staff completes a full extra rotation before settling back to out.
guide_l2_double_static_thumb: A base static motion has no thumb switches. With two turns it has two (in → out → in).
guide_l2_double_shifts_intro: Two turns add a 360° rotation to a motion.
guide_l2_double_shifts_pro_intro: With a double-turn prospin, notice the 45° angle at the halfway position.
guide_l2_double_shifts_pro_caption: Prospin with two turns: the staff rotates twice along one arc from east to south.
guide_l2_double_shifts_pro_thumb: A base prospin (ASA isolation) has no thumb switches. With two turns it has two (in → out → in).
guide_l2_double_shifts_anti_intro: A double-turn antispin is easier to see in thirds. At each third, a staff end reaches the center.
guide_l2_double_shifts_anti_caption: Antispin with two turns in thirds: the staff turns against its arc from east to south.
guide_l2_double_shifts_anti_thumb: A base antispin has one thumb switch (in → out). With two turns it has three (in → out → in → out).
guide_l2_double_dashes_intro: Add two turns to a dash. Break this complex motion into four parts.
guide_l2_double_dashes_quarters: Shown in quarters: watch the staff rotate as the hand travels straight from south to north.
guide_l2_double_dashes_thumb: A base dash starts thumb in and ends thumb out. With two turns it also ends thumb out (in → out).
guide_l2_double_dashes_direction: For a vertical dash, track the direction (up → down → up).
guide_l2_double_dashes_path: Keep the hand path straight while the prop turns. Here is the motion in halves:
guide_l2_double_dashes_halves: Shown in halves: the staff has completed a full rotation by the midpoint.

verified_level1_placements_intro:
There are multiple ways to combine two hand points to form a hand placement.
Placements can be rotated or mirrored.Red = Right and Blue = Left.
In The Kinetic Alphabet, our first three placements are called Alpha, Beta, and Gamma.
verified_level1_alpha_definition: In Alpha, the hands occupy the points across from each other.
verified_level1_beta_definition: In Beta, the hands occupy the same point.
verified_level1_gamma_definition: In Gamma, the hands form a right angle.

There are three fundamental hand motions in the Alphabet.
The arrow shows the direction of motion.
The hand shows the end position.
verified_level1_hand_motions_76:
Using these, we can derive six combinations, named below.
We’ll explore each one individually:

Gamma, aka quarter-time, is based on two often forgotten modes:
Quarter-Opp and Quarter-Same.
Quarter-Opp has variations of parallel and antiparallel.

Our first Dual-Shifts correspond to the four modes of time/direction: SS, TS, SO, TO.

verified_level1_lt2_wxyz_192:
So far we’ve learned how to move between α↔β and between γ↔γ.
In order to travel between these two modes, we can use a Type 2 Motion called a Shift.
verified_level1_lt2_wxyz_193:
A Shift (or single shift) is the combination of one shift and one static motion.
Their letters are organized by end position: α, β, then γ.
These can also be categorized by opening or closing.
verified_level1_lt2_wxyz_198: When we arrange them in continuous motions, we get the words WΣYΘ and XΔZΩ.
verified_level1_lt2_wxyz_201:
Though simple at this stage, these motions become more complex
as we dive deeper into the Alphabet and add rotations to static motions.
verified_level1_lt3_dash_letters_203:
Cross-Shifts use the same letters as Shifts, but each letter is followed by a
dash to indicate that the other hand is dashing into its end position.
They are spoken as “W Dash” or “Sigma Dash”.
A dash symbol in the glyph equals a dash arrow on the graph.
The end position for each Type 2/3 letter remains the same.
verified_level1_lt3_dash_letters_208:
Cross-Shifts can be tricky to remember. It helps to first picture the corresponding
Type 2 pictograph, then add the dash arrow without changing any other variables.
verified_level1_lt3_dash_letters_209: Just like we did with hands, let’s break down some Cross-Shifts step-by-step.
verified_level1_lt3_dash_letters_212: When initially learning, it’s useful to pause at the halfway point to ensure proper timing.

verified_level1_negative_space_229:
Many sequences seem impossible, but most can be solved by using negative space or body turns.
Negative space lets you face the audience and reduces body movement
Body turns add movement and help you execute patterns with longer staves.
Each method is equally important, and learning both will maximize capability.
This guide will assume some knowledge of these fundamental concepts.

verified_level1_negative_space_233: To execute this without finger-spinning, turn your torso to the left on step 3. During this step, the staff moves briefly in wheel-plane relative to your left-facing view. On step 4, turn your body back to center as you return to the start position.
verified_level1_negative_space_234:
Practice in reverse, then do both directions in the other hand.
Then practice it with the thumb out, isolating the pinky end.
verified_level1_negative_space_236: To execute this in wall plane, you must do one of the following on step 2:
verified_level1_negative_space_237:
• Pass the thumb end through the negative space above your right shoulder on step 2.
• Turn your torso to the left on step 2 and pass the thumb end in front, then pass the pinky end on the inside of your right arm as you move to step 3.
verified_level1_negative_space_238:
Practice in reverse, then do both directions in the other hand.
Then practice everything again starting with the thumb out.
Try using both negative space and turns. Good luck!
verified_level1_permutations_240:
When a word ends on a variation of its start position, we can repeat it to trace a
complimentary pattern, eventually returning back to the start position (aka home).
This type of sequence is called a LOOP.
verified_level1_permutations_241: Three common types of LOOPs are Mirrored, Rotated, and Swapped.
verified_level1_permutations_242: In a mirrored LOOP, the second repetition’s pictographs reflect the first, which changes their rotation direction.
verified_level1_permutations_243: In this example, each column is reflected across a horizontal plane.
verified_level1_permutations_244: In a rotated LOOP, each repetition ends in a rotated variation on its previous position.
verified_level1_permutations_246: In this example, there is a 90° rotation, finally returning to the start position (aka “home”).
verified_level1_permutations_248: In a swapped LOOP, each repetition swaps the roles of right/left.
verified_level1_permutations_249: Though the prop’s shapes look the same, this swap changes the body motion significantly.
verified_level1_prop_reversal_loops_251:
Each of these words uses a prop-reversal.
These examples are Rotated LOOPs.
verified_level1_prop_reversal_loops_255:
In this example of BΔMX, the right hand stops on steps 2 and 4 before resuming its motion around the center point. Even when there is a step with no motion in
between, we can still mark the reversal with an “R” to indicate the prop reversal.
verified_level1_reversals_261:
Reversals open up a huge number of possibilities!
There are three types of reversals:
verified_level1_reversals_262: With a hand reversal, the hand returns to the point it came from previously, without changing the prop’s direction of spin. Relative to the center point, this changes a prospin to an antispin and vice-versa.
verified_level1_reversals_263: This is the simplest and least disruptive reversal. We’ve already used it in the previous examples.
verified_level1_reversals_264: With a prop reversal, the hand continues to the next point while the prop reverses direction. This reversal also changes a prospin into an antispin and vice-versa.
verified_level1_reversals_265: Since a prop reversal is less intuitive, an “R/R” is shown in the corresponding color on the pictograph to indicate it.
verified_level1_reversals_266: With a full-reversal, the prop and hand retrace their paths and return to their previous position, as if going backwards in time.
verified_level1_reversals_267: Because this contains a prop reversal, the “R/R” draws attention to it. This succinctly indicates to the performer that something unusual is happening.
verified_level1_sixteen_count_269: These 4-letter words repeat 4 times, giving us 16-count sequences.
verified_level1_sixteen_count_270: Here, each repetition of the word ends in a β that is 90° from its start. This means it will take 4 repetitions to return to home.
verified_level1_sixteen_count_272: Here, the staves return to home after two word repetitions. To make it symmetrical, it repeats twice more, filling the rest of the quadrants.
verified_level1_staff_motions_275: During a shift, a prop can rotate in one of two directions - Prospin or Antispin
verified_level1_staff_motions_277:
• Prospin - The prop rotates the same direction as the handpath
A 90 degree isolation is our base unit of a prospin.
verified_level1_staff_motions_279: In a base isolation, the thumb orientation remains the same for the entire motion.
verified_level1_staff_motions_281:
• Antispin - The prop rotates in the opposite direction of the handpath
A 90 degree antispin is our base unit of antispin.
verified_level1_staff_motions_282: In an antispin, the ends swap orientation. Here, it moves from thumb in to thumb out.
verified_level1_staff_motions_283: In a base dash, the thumb ends also swap orientation.
verified_level1_staff_motions_284: Halfway through the motion, the center of the staff is at the grid’s center point.
verified_level1_staff_placements_286:
When writing sequences with staves, it helps to mark the thumb end with a line.
The performer can use it to keep track of rotations and check their position on every step.
It also encourages negative space/body turns instead of finger spinning.
verified_level1_staff_placements_287: In the following examples, an end is always at the center point.
verified_level1_staff_placements_288: Practice each placement below, paying attention to the thumb orientation.
verified_level1_staff_placements_289: Thumbs: in out (out/in) (in/out)
verified_level1_staff_placements_290:
Many of the pictographs in this guide are depicted with no thumb ends
when categorizing. It is usually noted only during sequences.
verified_level1_staff_placements_291:
Most sequences in this guide start with thumbs in for consistency.
It’s equally valid to start any sequence from a different thumb orientation.
verified_level1_type2_loops_293: These words use the Type 2 letters to travel between α/β and γ.
verified_level1_type2_loops_294: Since each repetition is rotated by 180°, these are all Rotated LOOPs.
verified_level1_type2_loops_295: BΣTX is the print example for this slot: a Rotated LOOP that travels between alpha and gamma.
verified_level1_type2_loops_296: EΔUZ is the print example for this slot: a Rotated LOOP that travels between beta and gamma.
verified_level1_type2_loops_297: OYHΘ is the print example for this slot: a Rotated LOOP that travels between gamma and beta.
verified_level1_words_302: Let’s create more complex words using pictographs!
verified_level1_words_303:
In order to perform the words in this section correctly without finger-spinning,
you must be familiar with negative space and body turns.
verified_level1_words_304:
If you finger-spin instead of using negative space, you’ll lose precision and
the ability to check your thumb orientation on each step to see if you’re still on track.
verified_level1_words_305:
We’ll use the word AABB as an example. Here are three variations on AABB, starting from
different thumb orientations. Use staves or red/blue pens to follow along.
verified_level1_words_309:
As you execute these with staves, notice that each of these sequences requires a different type
of negative space, either above/below the shoulder or behind the elbow.
verified_level1_words_310:
The execution of the same word can feel completely different depending on factors like
the start position, rotation direction, and thumb orientation. That’s why it’s necessary to
draw the full sequence with pictographs for complete clarity.
verified_level1_words_311:
The Alphabet is primarily a system of pictographs,
organized by letters for convenient communication.
verified_level1_words_312:
The letters do not give all of the information, and are merely intended to separate
motion combinations into categories which can be further clarified with detailed pictographs.

guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_0: A glyph is a letter combined with other characters, such as numbers or symbols.
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_1:
To the right of each letter, there are two slots - high and low.
These slots contain numbers that indicate turns.
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_2:
In a hybrid, motion types are
different and must be disambiguated.
These rules indicate where to place numbers:
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_3: The motion that is higher on the list is indicated by the high slot.
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_4: Remember the order with the acronym PADS, for Pro, Anti, Dash, Static.
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_5:
The letters S and T have another factor - leading/following.
In their case, leading is high and following is low.
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_6: There are five hybrids, each shown below in their corresponding high/low slots.
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_7: The remaining letters have combinations of the same motion type.
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_8: For these, put left in the high slot and right in the low slot.
guide_l2_print_glyphspadspage_9:
These letters include:
A, B, D, E, G, H, J, K, M, N, P, Q, S, T
Φ-, Ψ-, Λ-
α, β, Γ
guide_l2_print_turnspage_0: A turn is a 180° rotation that occurs during a motion.
guide_l2_print_turnspage_1: Let’s add a single turn to a shift.
guide_l2_print_turnspage_2:
First we’ll add 1 turn to a prospin.
Take note of the diagonal halfway position, and pause there for a moment before continuing.
These arrows refer to the pinky end on the first half, then to the thumb end on the second half.
The full arrow depicts a half-circle, from the start position’s outer point.
guide_l2_print_turnspage_3: Each turn adds a thumb switch.
guide_l2_print_turnspage_4:
An isolation has 0 thumb switches, therefore
A prospin with a turn has 1 thumb switch (in → out)
guide_l2_print_turnspage_5:
Now let’s add 1 turn to an antispin.
Again, take note of the diagonal halfway position, and pause there before continuing.
guide_l2_print_turnspage_6:
A base antispin has 1 thumb switch. (in → out), therefore
An antispin with a turn has 2 thumb switches (in → out → in).
guide_l2_print_dashstaticturnspage_0:
You can also add a turn to a dash.
During the prop rotation, move the hand directly in a straight line.
Pause at the halfway point while learning to ensure that your hand is in
the center point and the staff is perpendicular to your starting position.
guide_l2_print_dashstaticturnspage_1:
A base dash has 1 thumb switch (in → out), therefore:
A dash with a turn has 2 thumb switches (in → in)
guide_l2_print_dashstaticturnspage_2:
Executing this move on repeat is commonly called a linear extension.
It feels peculiar to execute with staves because one end is in pro and the other end is in anti.
guide_l2_print_dashstaticturnspage_3:
It helps to focus on the half that’s in antispin.
This will ensure that you pass your hand directly through the center point.
guide_l2_print_dashstaticturnspage_4:
Finally, we’ll look at static turns.
Here is a breakdown of a static turn starting from thumb in:
guide_l2_print_dashstaticturnspage_5:
This can be executed at any hand point, starting from either
thumb orientation, turning in either direction.
guide_l2_print_dashstaticturnspage_6: Note the differences between the arrow for static turns and the arrow for prospin turns:
guide_l2_print_twoturnsshiftspage_0: 2 turns add a 360 degree rotation to a motion.
guide_l2_print_twoturnsshiftspage_1: On a prospin with a double turn, note the 45° angle of the halfway position.
guide_l2_print_twoturnsshiftspage_2:
A base prospin (ASA isolation) has 0 thumb switches, therefore
A prospin with 2 turns has 2 thumb switch (in → out → in)
guide_l2_print_twoturnsshiftspage_3:
With a double-turning antispin, it’s easier to visually conceive of the motion in thirds
At each third there is a staff end at the center point.
guide_l2_print_twoturnsshiftspage_4:
A base antispin has 1 thumb switch. (in → out), therefore
An antispin with 2 turns has 3 thumb switches (in → out → in → out).
guide_l2_print_twoturnsshiftspage_5: Here is the same motion broken in half:
guide_l2_print_twoturnsdashstaticpage_0:
Now let’s add a double turn to a dash.
It’s relatively complex, so we’ll break it down into four parts.
(These arrows refer to the pinky end on the first half,
then to the thumb end on the second half.)
guide_l2_print_twoturnsdashstaticpage_1:
As with all dashes, it’s important to travel in a straight handpath even though the prop is rotating.
Here is the same motion broken in half:
guide_l2_print_twoturnsdashstaticpage_2:
A base dash starting from thumb in ends with thumb out, therefore
A dash with 2 turns also ends with thumb out. (in → out)
For a vertical dash such as this, you can use up/down as indicators. (up → down → up)
guide_l2_print_twoturnsdashstaticpage_3:
Finally, a static motion with 2 turns is simply a 360° turn in place.
It’s necessary to use negative space or a turn to achieve this.
guide_l2_print_twoturnsdashstaticpage_4:
A static motion has 0 thumb switches, therefore
A static motion with 2 turns has 2 thumb switches (in → out → in).
guide_l2_print_openingclosingpage_0:
Because of Gamma’s asymmetry, Λ (Lam) presents an extra variation when adding a turn.
We can’t use rotational relationship to tell them apart, because there isn’t one to describe.
Instead, we can disambiguate them with opening and closing.
This refers to the appearance of the 90° angle if we continue the rotation into a pro-shift.
guide_l2_print_openingclosingpage_1: Take a look at the sequences below and their hypothetical continuation. Note the difference.
guide_l2_print_openingclosingpage_2: Now let’s add 1 turn to the static hand, leaving the dash in its base form.
guide_l2_print_openingclosingpage_3:
Since the dashing prop is not rotating, there is no rotational relationship to describe.
However the rotating static prop can still be identified as opening or closing.
guide_l2_print_openingclosingpage_4:
It’s not necessary to speak all of the glyph modifications when talking about a letter.
It would be cumbersome if you were required to say “Lam-Low-One-Closing”.
In the context of a word or sequence, you can just refer to the base letter “Lam” instead.
guide_l2_print_openingclosingpage_5: To shorten this for code, include “op” or “cl” as a final parameter. E.g. “Λ(0,1,op)” or “Λ(0,1,cl)”
guide_l2_print_sandtpage_0: S and T are a different type of hybrid.
guide_l2_print_sandtpage_1: Even though their motions are a matching shift type (pro|pro, anti|anti), each has one hand leading and the other following. Though this doesn’t affect their base forms, it produces additional variations when modifying their motions.
guide_l2_print_sandtpage_2: S and T are the only letters with this unique quality.
guide_l2_print_sandtpage_3: Fortunately, we have a tool to disambiguate hybrids - the high/low slots.
guide_l2_print_sandtpage_4:
For S and T,
high = leading and low = following.
guide_l2_print_sandtpage_5: Note that these leading/following rules do NOT apply to U and V.
guide_l2_print_sandtpage_6: Even though U and V have a leader/follower, their slots refer to pro/anti.
guide_l2_print_type1dualshiftpage_0:
When motion types are exactly the same,
put left in the high slot and right in the low slot.
Here is a breakdown of A1 (pro|pro) and B1 (anti|anti).
guide_l2_print_type1dualshiftpage_1:
When motion types are different, high/low indicates how to label them.
With hybrids, we can add a turn to either the pro or anti motion.
guide_l2_print_type1dualshiftpage_2:
For pro/anti hybrids,
high = prospin and low = antispin,
guide_l2_print_type1dualshiftpage_3: This includes C, F, I, L, O, R, U, and V.
guide_l2_print_type1dualshiftpage_4: For code or file-naming, indicate turns with parentheses like so:  C<sup>1</sup> = C(1,0) and C<sub>1</sub> = C(0,1)
guide_l2_print_type2shiftpage_0:
Type 2 hybrids combine a shift and a static motion.
These two motion types are different, so we use the high/low slots to differentiate them.
To determine where they go, remember PADS.
Because a shift (pro/anti) is higher than a static motion, we can confidently state that:
guide_l2_print_type2shiftpage_1:
For Type 2,
high = shift and low = static.
guide_l2_print_type2shiftpage_2: This includes W, X, Y, Z, Σ, Δ, Θ, and Ω.
guide_l2_print_type2shiftpage_3: Let’s add 1 high turn to a Type 2 motion, which only affects the shift.
guide_l2_print_type2shiftpage_4: Since the static hand is still, this should be simple to execute.
guide_l2_print_type2shiftpage_5:
Type 2 motions become more complex when we add turns to the static hand.
Since this causes both props to rotate, it creates either a Same or Opposite relationship.
To indicate this, add a dot above or below the letter.*
guide_l2_print_type2shiftpage_6: A same-dot goes above and an opp-dot goes below.
guide_l2_print_type2shiftpage_7: You can also use (s) or (o) as parameters to indicate “same” or “opp”. E.g. “W(s,0,1)”
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_0:
Type 3 hybrids combine a shift with a dash.
When we consult PADS, we find that a shift is higher than a dash, therefore:
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_1:
For Type 3,
high = shift and low = dash.
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_2: This includes W-, X-, Y-, Z-, Σ-, Δ-, Θ-, and Ω-.
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_3: First, we’ll add 1 high turn to Z-, which only affects the shift.
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_4: Take note of this strange position at the halfway point.
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_5:
There is a hand-to-end relationship between the left hand and the right staff’s pinky end.
It is important to pass through this position for the timing to be accurate.
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_6:
Now let’s add 1 turn to the dash, leaving the shifting hand unmodified.
This creates a rotational relationship, so we’ll need to use Same-dots and Opp-dots.
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_7: The halfway position holds the key for executing cross-shifts with accurate timing.
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_8: Though unfamiliar now, these centric positions will be thoroughly deconstructed later on.
guide_l2_print_type3crossshiftpage_9: When writing code, put the dash after the letter and before the parentheses. “E.g. Z-(s,0,1)”
guide_l2_print_type4dashpage_0:
Type 4 hybrids combine a dash with a static motion. There is no shift involved.
According to PADS, a dash is higher than a static motion.
We reflect that by using the high slot for dash and the low slot for static.
guide_l2_print_type4dashpage_1:
For Type 4,
high = dash and low = static.
guide_l2_print_type4dashpage_2: This includes Φ, Ψ, and Λ.
guide_l2_print_type4dashpage_4:
Since only one prop is rotating, there is no rotational relationship to describe.
If we follow the same dash while rotating in the opposite direction,
the pictograph is a mirror image and needs no disambiguation.
guide_l2_print_type4dashpage_5: Now let’s add 1 turn to the static hand, leaving the dash in its base form.
guide_l2_print_type4dashpage_6: Pause at the halfway point and check your position.
guide_l2_print_type4dashpage_7:
Here, there is a hand-to-end relationship with the left hand and the right pinky end.
Again, there is no rotational relationship to describe,
so we don’t need to separate them.
guide_l2_print_type4dashpage_8:
When typing the words for sequences containing greek symbols,
it’s easier to just type the word or its first three letters. E.g. “phi(0,1)”
The corresponding symbol can easily be swapped in with a simple script.
The short versions of the seven greek letters are “sig, del, the, om, phi, psi, lam”
guide_l2_print_type5dualdashpage_0:
In Type 5 motions, both hands are dashing, so there are no hybrids.
Since they’re the same type (dash|dash), the left goes in the high slot,
and the right goes in the low slot.
guide_l2_print_type5dualdashpage_1: This includes Φ-, Ψ-, and Λ-.
guide_l2_print_type5dualdashpage_3: Remember - the high/low slots do not refer to left/right.
guide_l2_print_type5dualdashpage_4:
Instead, their purpose is to differentiate two motion types.
In Type 5, those motion types are the same (dash|dash).
guide_l2_print_type5dualdashpage_5: Now let’s look at Λ-1, which again presents variations of opening and closing.
guide_l2_print_type5dualdashpage_6:
As always, pause at the halfway point to drill it into your muscle memory.
This will ensure proper timing.
guide_l2_print_type6staticpage_0:
Finally, Type 6 letters have both hands remaining static.
Both types are the same (static|static), so the number goes in the high slot by default.
guide_l2_print_type6staticpage_1: This includes α, β, and Γ.
guide_l2_print_type6staticpage_3:
Note that the arrow can follow the path of either the thumb end or pinky end.
The optimal placement depends on context.
guide_l2_print_type6staticpage_5:
These static single-turns are relatively simple.
Next we’ll look at dual-turns, in which both props are receiving a turn.

create_action_help_mirror_fulldesc: Creates a mirror image of your sequence, as if mirrored across the vertical center line. All movements that go left now go right, and vice versa. Clockwise turns become counter-clockwise. You can combine this with other transforms for unique variations.
create_action_help_flip_fulldesc: Flips your sequence vertically, as if mirrored across the horizontal center line. All movements that go up (north) now go down (south), and vice versa. Clockwise turns become counter-clockwise. Great for creating vertical variations of your sequences.
create_action_help_invert_fulldesc: Inverts all rotation directions and motion types in your sequence. Every clockwise turn becomes counter-clockwise (and vice versa), and every PRO motion becomes ANTI (and vice versa). The movement paths stay the same, but the way you spin changes. This creates new letters since rotation direction and motion type are part of what defines each letter.
create_action_help_rotate_fulldesc: Rotates the entire sequence 45° as if you physically turned your body. N becomes NE (clockwise) or NW (counter-clockwise). Tap the arrows to rotate clockwise or counter-clockwise. Rotate 4 times in the same direction for a full 180°.
create_action_help_swap_fulldesc: Exchanges all left-hand movements with right-hand movements. Your sequence looks the same, but the opposite hand now performs each movement. Great for creating mirror variations or practicing both sides.
create_action_help_rewind_fulldesc: Like rewinding a video! Takes the end placement as your new start, then plays every step backwards. Turns flip direction (clockwise becomes counter-clockwise). Note: This will change the letters or word of your sequence!
create_action_help_turn_pattern_fulldesc: Applies a turn pattern across your entire sequence. Turn patterns let you create consistent rhythms by setting how many turns (0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, or 3) each step has. Choose from presets like 'All Half Turns' or 'Alternating 1-2' or create your own custom pattern.
create_action_help_direction_fulldesc: Sets the rotation direction pattern for your sequence. Control whether each step rotates clockwise (CW) or counter-clockwise (CCW). Choose from presets like 'All Clockwise', 'Alternating', or create custom direction patterns for each step.
create_action_help_duration_fulldesc: Controls how long each beat is held. Apply rhythmic patterns like 'Every Third Doubled' (beats 3, 6, 9 hold twice as long), 'Swing' (triplet feel), or musical meters like 'Waltz' or 'Shuffle'. Use uniform buttons to speed up (50%, 25%) or slow down (150%, 200%, 400%) your entire sequence.
create_action_help_extend_fulldesc: Extends your sequence back to its starting placement using a LOOP pattern. When the last step's placement matches the first step's placement group, you can choose from different LOOP types (like Mirrored, Swapped, or Rotated) to loop your sequence.
create_action_help_shift_start_fulldesc: Changes where the sequence starts. While choosing, every tile shows only the pose it ends in. Tap the pose you want to start from and the sequence reorders to begin there. Sequences that don't loop drop the steps before it.
create_action_help_invert_warning: This will change the letters in your sequence!
create_action_detail_mirror: Flips horizontally, like looking in a mirror. Left becomes right, clockwise becomes counter-clockwise.
create_action_detail_flip: Flips vertically, like turning upside down. Up becomes down, clockwise becomes counter-clockwise.
create_action_detail_invert: Inverts rotation relative to the path. Pro becomes Anti, and Anti becomes Pro. Base motion types remain unchanged.
create_action_detail_swap: Exchanges left and right hand movements. Same pattern, opposite hands perform each motion.
create_action_detail_rewind: Plays backwards. End becomes start, every step reverses order, turns flip direction.
